reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: 2015 update of the FHWA driven pile manual (earlier editions 1985, 1997 and 2006), revised to incorporate LRFD methodology per AASHTO. Key updates include soil setup quantification, improved equipment monitoring, higher-strength materials, instrumented load tests, and enhanced QA/QC methods.
sections.body: (p. 1) In 1985 the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) published the first edition of this manual. Subsequent editions were published in 1997 and 2006. This 2015 update is primarily dictated by the need to revise and update manual content in accordance with the Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) methodology which replaced the Allowable Strength Design (ASD) method for the design of transportation substructures in 2007. Other changes in practice addressed by this edition: a rational economic evaluation of the foundation design, higher strength pile materials and larger driven sections for greater loads, updated computer programs, the use and quantification of soil setup, improved installation equipment and equipment performance monitoring, more instrumented static load test programs, and improved QA/QC methods for nominal resistance and pile integrity verification.
key_points: Emphasis on rational economic evaluation of foundation design
Use of higher strength pile materials and/or larger driven pile sections
Updates in computer programs for pile foundation analysis and design
Use and quantification of soil setup in pile design and construction
Improvements in pile installation equipment and equipment performance monitoring
Increased use of instrumented static load test programs
Improvements in QA/QC methods for nominal resistance and pile integrity verifications
sections.applicability: General introduction to the GEC-12 manual and changes from previous editions.

sections.title: Purpose of the Manual
sections.summary: Nine purposes: compile scattered driven pile information in a form useful to practicing engineers; replace unnecessarily conservative experience-based methods with rational procedures; save at least fifteen percent of substructure cost through improved design and construction; give a comprehensive LRFD driven pile manual with minimum standards; address extreme events, lateral and uplift loading, group behavior and deformation criteria; combined axial and bending structural analysis; alternative contracting; cost evaluation including soil setup; and the wider range of hammers.
sections.body: (pp. 1-3) The purposes of earlier editions remain largely unchanged and are restated as nine points: (1) much proven information on driven piles (rational design procedures, materials, equipment, techniques, case histories) is fragmented, and textbooks lack practical aspects; (2) many historical methods are unnecessarily conservative, being based on experience and tradition, and rational procedures give more economical foundations; (3) improved design and construction methods can easily save a minimum of fifteen percent of the substructure cost, often more; (4) with LRFD adopted for all transportation projects a comprehensive manual is needed, and this one also sets minimum design standards and recommendations; (5) extreme events (scour, debris, vessel impact, seismic) require evaluation under lateral and uplift loading, group behavior and substructure-superstructure interaction, with deformation criteria now routine; (6) combined horizontal and axial loads require a combined bending and axial structural analysis, for concrete piles an ultimate strength analysis, rather than the old allowable stress approach set for drivability; (7) alternative contracting methods (design-build, CM/GC) are replacing design-bid-build and challenge existing specifications; (8) final pile selection should involve a cost evaluation including soil setup effects; (9) more hammer types and sizes and better installation aids allow efficient installation in most conditions.
key_points: Compiles fragmented driven pile information in a form useful to practicing engineers
Replaces unnecessarily conservative, experience-based methods with rational design procedures
A minimum of fifteen percent of the substructure cost can be easily saved by improved methods
A comprehensive LRFD driven pile manual that also sets minimum design standards and recommendations
Extreme events require lateral, uplift, group and substructure-superstructure evaluation; deformation criteria are routine
Combined bending and axial structural analysis is required; for concrete piles an ultimate strength analysis
Alternative contracting methods (design-build, CM/GC) are replacing design-bid-build
Final pile design selection should involve a cost evaluation, including the effects of soil setup
A larger selection of hammer types and sizes and better installation aids allow efficient installation
sections.applicability: All driven pile foundation projects for highway structures.

sections.title: Scope of Manual
sections.summary: The manual is limited to driven piles: eighteen chapters and four appendices. The first half covers design (cost evaluation, geotechnical data collection and analysis, pile type selection, geotechnical and structural limit state design); the second half covers nominal resistance verification, pile driving equipment, accessories and inspection. Theory only where necessary; recommendations and example problems are given. A standalone document, with a separate training course.
sections.body: (pp. 3-4) The manual is limited to driven piles and consists of eighteen chapters and four appendices. The first half covers the design aspects of pile foundations: cost evaluations, geotechnical data collection and analysis, selection of pile type, and the geotechnical and structural aspects of limit state design. The second half covers methods of nominal resistance verification and chapters on pile driving equipment, accessories and inspection procedures. Theoretical discussions are included only where necessary, specific recommendations are made where appropriate, and example problems give hands-on knowledge. The manual is a standalone document; a separate training course transfers the knowledge, continuing the goal of updating transportation department practice and training new engineers in practical pile design and installation.
key_points: Limited to driven piles: eighteen chapters and four appendices
First half: design (cost evaluation, geotechnical data, pile type selection, geotechnical and structural limit state design)
Second half: nominal resistance verification, pile driving equipment, accessories and inspection
Theoretical discussions only where necessary; specific recommendations and example problems provided
A standalone document, with a separate training course
sections.applicability: Defines the scope and organization of the two-volume manual.

sections.title: History of Driven Pile Foundations
sections.summary: Driven timber piles may date to 800 BC (mauls or drop hammers). Reinforced concrete piles: Europe 1897, Chicago 1901; steel piles followed; precast prestressed and 36 and 54 inch post-tensioned cylinder piles in the 1950s. Naysmith's steam hammer patented 1839; diesel hammer, Germany, mid 1920s; vibratory hammers, Soviet Union 1940s, U.S. 1960s; hydraulic hammers, Scandinavia 1960s; Bodine's resonant driver 1960s, re-emerged in the 2000s.
sections.body: (p. 4) The detailed history has been lost; some of the earliest driven timber piles may date to 800 BC, installed with mauls or drop hammers. Reinforced concrete piles debuted in Europe in 1897 and in Chicago in 1901; structural steel piles (pipe, I-beams, H-piles) followed. Octagonal and square precast prestressed concrete piles and 36 inch and 54 inch diameter post-tensioned concrete cylinder piles developed in the 1950s. The first modern pile hammer was a Scottish steam hammer patented by Naysmith in 1839; steam hammers were reported in the U.S. between the mid and late 1800s. The diesel hammer was invented in Germany in the mid 1920s. Vibratory hammers were invented in the Soviet Union in the 1940s and reached the U.S. market in the 1960s. The first hydraulic hammers were developed in Scandinavia in the 1960s. Bodine developed a resonant pile hammer in the 1960s, little used for mechanical reliability reasons; the resonant driver re-emerged in the 2000s. Rausche (2000) summarized the development of pile driving equipment.
key_points: Driven timber piles may date back to 800 BC, installed with mauls or drop hammers
Reinforced concrete piles: Europe 1897, Chicago 1901; structural steel piles followed
Precast prestressed piles and 36 and 54 inch post-tensioned cylinder piles developed in the 1950s
First modern hammer: Naysmith's Scottish steam hammer, patented 1839; diesel hammer, Germany, mid 1920s
Vibratory hammers: invented in the Soviet Union in the 1940s, U.S. market in the 1960s
Hydraulic hammers: Scandinavia, 1960s; resonant driver (Bodine) 1960s, re-emerged in the 2000s
sections.applicability: Historical context for driven pile foundation practice.

sections.title: Information Sources
sections.summary: Primary reference: AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications 7th Ed. (2014) with 2015 Interim Revisions. Key supporting references: GEC-5 (Soil & Rock Properties), GEC-10 (Drilled Shafts), GEC-3 (LRFD Seismic), and HEC-18 (Scour at Bridges).
sections.body: (pp. 4-5) Primary references are the 7th Edition of the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (2014) with 2015 Interim Revisions and the 3rd Edition of the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Construction Specifications with 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2014 Interim Revisions. Additional sources include GEC-5 (Evaluation of Soil and Rock Properties, Sabatini et al. 2002), Implementation of AASHTO LRFD Design Specifications for Driven Piles (Abu-Hejleh et al. 2013), GEC-10 (Drilled Shafts, Brown et al. 2010), GEC-3 (LRFD Seismic Analysis, Kavazanjian et al. 2011) and HEC-18 (Evaluating Scour at Bridges, Arneson et al. 2012), plus technical publications, manufacturers' literature, FHWA, NHI and TRB publications, textbooks and information from transportation engineers. Reference lists close each chapter.
